metadata.file_name: 16. Bernardo et al. (2021). Using Machine Learning Approaches to Explore Non-Cognitive Variables Influencing Reading Proficiency in English among Filipino Learners.pdf
metadata.title: Using Machine Learning Approaches to Explore Non-Cognitive Variables Influencing Reading Proficiency in English among Filipino Learners

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines national sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) downloaded as a public-use file from OECD. The original PISA design is described as a two-stage stratified random selection of schools (187 schools across 17 regions) followed by random sampling of students within schools, but the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/testing pipeline. For modeling, the authors rescaled variables to 0–1, imputed missing values using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), and then trained multiple classifiers on an 80/20 random split with five-fold cross-validation for training performance. Because the paper does not state weight usage, the safest interpretation is that complex survey weighting was not incorporated into the ML estimation, which may limit population-representativeness and under/over-estimate uncertainty under the nested school design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the complete nationally representative PISA 2018 Philippines student sample (7233 15-year-olds) selected via two-stage stratified sampling (187 schools across 17 regions). For ML, students were labeled into low vs high reading proficiency groups using PV1 for reading (low = Levels 1b and below; high = Levels 1a and above). From the 122 candidate variables, variables with 100% missingness were dropped; remaining variables with missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbors with k=7 after converting PISA missing tags ("M"/"N") to nulls. Variables were rescaled to 0–1 prior to model training.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) Reading — PV1READ-based low vs high proficiency
main_findings.target_variable: Reading proficiency group (low Levels 1b and below vs high Levels 1a and above) using PV1READ
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (RBF kernel) — best average test accuracy: 81.20%; AUC-ROC: 0.89. Worst AUC-ROC reported: 0.5; best AUC-ROC reported: 1.0. Five-fold cross-validation used for training performance; hyperparameters selected via grid search.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Philippines reading the study leveraged SCREADDIFF, BEINGBULLIED, WORKMAST, ICTRES, and JOYREAD to classify students into low vs high reading proficiency groups, finding that the SVM achieved the best test performance (accuracy 81.20%, AUC-ROC 0.89) and that higher perceived reading difficulty and bullying exposure were associated with low proficiency while mastery motivation was associated with higher proficiency. This indicates that interventions targeting reading self-beliefs (reducing perceived difficulty), school social climate (bullying reduction and belonging/cooperation), and mastery-oriented motivation may be high-leverage for improving English reading outcomes among Filipino students, though the results are predictive and not causal and may be sensitive to the unreported use of PISA sampling weights.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Philippines data (7233 students) and predicts a binary reading proficiency label derived from PV1READ: low proficiency corresponds to Levels 1b and below, while high corresponds to Levels 1a and above. After converting PISA missing tags to nulls, the authors dropped variables with 100% missingness and imputed remaining missing values using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), then rescaled variables to 0–1. Multiple classifiers were trained and tuned via grid search, with five-fold cross-validation for training performance and an 80/20 random split for testing. The SVM with an RBF kernel performed best, reaching 81.20% test accuracy and AUC-ROC of 0.89, outperforming other models including logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, AdaBoost, and kNN. Interpretation relies on SHAP for feature importance, but the paper’s predictive focus and the lack of explicit reporting on survey-weight use mean results should be treated as correlational and potentially limited in generalizability under the nested PISA design.
